title: Injera
subtitle: ethiopian fermented teff flatbread
excerpt: A sour, spongy flatbread that doubles as plate and utensil across Ethiopia. Ferment the batter overnight for the best flavour.
sourceNotes: Traditional Ethiopian household recipe. Teff is native to the Horn of Africa and has been cultivated there for thousands of years.

recipe.freezeNotes: Stack cooled injera between sheets of baking paper and freeze in a zip bag for up to one month. Reheat wrapped in a damp cloth in a low oven.
recipe.batchNotes: Double or triple the batter; cook in batches and stack once cool.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The batter must ferment for at least 12 hours and up to 24. Cooked injera keeps wrapped at room temperature for two days.

glossaryTerms.definition: Ethiopian fermented flatbread made from teff flour, used as both plate and utensil.

content.text: is a large, sour flatbread eaten at almost every Ethiopian meal. The batter ferments overnight, giving the bread its distinctive tang and hundreds of tiny bubbles on the surface. Those bubbles are what makes injera so good at soaking up stews.
Teff flour is gluten-free and nutty in flavour. If you cannot find it, plain flour labelled teff flour works as a substitute, though the colour will be lighter.

Whisk the teff flour and lukewarm water together in a large bowl until smooth. Cover loosely with a clean cloth and leave at room temperature for 12 to 24 hours to ferment. The batter should smell pleasantly sour and show small bubbles on the surface.
Stir the batter well. It should have the consistency of thin pancake batter. Add a little more water if it seems too thick.

Heat a 30 cm non-stick frying pan over medium-high heat. Brush lightly with vegetable oil. Once the pan is hot, pour in a ladleful of batter (about 120 ml) and immediately swirl the pan to spread the batter into a thin, even circle.
Cook without flipping for 2 to 3 minutes. The edges will lift and the surface will look dry with many small holes. Slide onto a clean surface and leave to cool flat. Do not stack while warm.
Repeat with the remaining batter, wiping and lightly re-oiling the pan between each injera. Serve at room temperature with stews spooned directly on top.

attrs.issue: Batter did not ferment or develop bubbles

content.text: A cold kitchen slows fermentation. Move the bowl somewhere warmer, such as near an oven or on top of a fridge. Give it another 6 hours before using.

attrs.issue: Injera tears when sliding out of the pan

content.text: The batter may be too thin or the pan too hot. Let the batter rest another hour and lower the heat slightly. The injera is ready to slide when the entire surface looks dry.
Re-oil the pan between each flatbread. Non-stick pans work best here. Cast iron can also be used if well seasoned.

Injera is eaten daily in Ethiopia and Eritrea. It lines the serving platter and replaces cutlery. Teff grows well in the Ethiopian highlands. The grain is tiny but packed with iron and protein. Injera is as central to the table there as bread is in Europe.
